title: The Montgomery Bus Boycott
text:
On 1 December 1955 Rosa Parks, a seamstress and longtime NAACP activist, was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger. That night Jo Ann Robinson, an English professor at Alabama State College and a leader of the Women's Political Council, went to the college with two students and spent the night mimeographing tens of thousands of leaflets calling on Black residents to stay off the buses on Monday, 5 December.

Nearly all of them did. That afternoon local leaders formed the Montgomery Improvement Association and chose a 26-year-old pastor new to the city, Martin Luther King Jr., as its president. That evening a packed church meeting voted to continue the boycott.

Keeping tens of thousands of people off the buses every day took organization. The association set up a carpool system with hundreds of private cars and dozens of pickup points, run like a transit service. Churches bought station wagons. Many people simply walked, some for miles, in all weather. When the city pressured Black taxi drivers and arrested carpool drivers, they kept going. King's house was bombed in January 1956, and nearly ninety leaders were indicted under an old anti-boycott law.

The boycott lasted 381 days. In November 1956 the US Supreme Court upheld a ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional. On 21 December 1956, King and others rode a Montgomery bus and sat at the front.
lesson: Collective action works when sacrifice is shared and well organized. Passion starts a movement; logistics and persistence carry it to the end.
people: Rosa Parks, Jo Ann Robinson, Martin Luther King Jr., E. D. Nixon, Montgomery Improvement Association
source: Jo Ann Gibson Robinson, The Montgomery Bus Boycott and the Women Who Started It (1987); Taylor Branch, Parting the Waters (1988)
place: Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery, Alabama
